text.p: Advanta Corp said it reached a "standstill" agreement with the Visa credit card association in its dispute over an Advanta-issued credit card tied to the American Express rewards program.

A spokeswoman said she was unable to provide any details because the agreement prohibits public comment. She said the agreement was reached to facilitate a resolution of the dispute by January 22, 1997.
A spokesman for the Visa card association was not immediately available for comment.

Earlier Tuesday, the Mastercard Internatonal card association said it filed suit against Advanta and American Express Co, alleging trademark infringement, unfair competition, breach of contract and tortuous interference with contractual relations. An American Express Co spokesman also was not available for comment.
The Rewards Accelerator card was the first such U.S. alliance between American Express and an issuer of credit cards on the Visa and Mastercard networks.

"In order to facilitate an orderly hearing and resolution of the preliminary injunction issues by January 22, 1997, the parties have agreed to a standstill agreement on both sides without prejudice to either side's rights," said a prepared statement by Advanta.
The Advanta spokeswoman declined to say if the standstill meant Advanta was no longer soliciting business for Rewards Accelerator cards tied to the Visa network.
Earlier this year, American Express chairman and chief executive Harvey Golub personally asked bankers to consider issuing American Express cards.
The Visa and Mastercard associations promptly criticized Golub's proposal as an attempt to divide the membership of the groups.
Although the Rewards Accelerator alliance was short of what Golub had proposed, industry analysts said it was an important foot in the door for American Express.

Robert McKlnley, president of RAM Research group, which tracks trends in the credit card industry, said the dispute actually achieves an objective of American Express by bringing the issue of competition in the card industry into the spotlight.
"American Express is not going to lose anything," McKinley said. "I think they're gloating over this."
He noted the Department of Justice is looking into industry practices.
McKinley said that, while it is difficult to predict the outcome of the litigation, "those with the most to lose are Visa and Mastercard."

In a later telephone call, a spokeswoman for American Express said the suit by Mastercard "has no merit." She said Visa and Mastercard dominate the market and attempts to prevent members from developing new products.
Later a Visa spokeswoman read the same statement released by Advanta concerning the standstill. She declined to answer an questions.

A source said that, apparently under the standstill, Advanta has stopped new solicitations for the Rewards Accelerator card on the Visa network, but was issuing cards to those who responded to earlier solicitations.
